prompt.context: A friend approaches you to invest in a software gaming company that he is starting. He is a programmer and has developed a computer game that he says 'will sell like hotcakes.' He wants you to make an investment of $500K. Your $500K will buy you a 50% stake in the company. (Assume he is taking a 50% stake in equity for his work in developing the game.) You consider investing, but have some other investment options that can potentially give you a 50% ROI over the next year with the same risk as this company. Assume this investment is a one-year investment and no money from the company will be reinvested for the following year.
prompt.question: Should you invest in your friend's company or in the other investment options that you have?

clarifying_info.q: How many people will be running the company and what will they earn this year?
clarifying_info.a: The founder has recruited two friends from business school to handle all aspects of running the company and marketing the product. They have prior experience in software sales. He is paying each of them $100,000 per year. The founder is not taking a salary, just his 50% equity stake.

clarifying_info.q: Are there similar products in the market / what does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are three companies that make similar games. There are six titles in all in this space. Each title currently has an equal share of the market.

clarifying_info.q: What are the manufacturing, packaging and shipping costs per unit?
clarifying_info.a: The company does not yet have that information — you will need to estimate it.

In their first year they will sell through retail stores (e.g., Best Buy). Retail stores take a 30% margin on the selling price. There is also a consumer marketing support charge from retailers that comes to 10% of selling price, which covers all costs necessary to market the product.
No, those are all the variable costs.
No, assume fixed costs are zero.

framework: Estimate the gaming company's first-year profitability to compare with the alternative 50% ROI investment
Step 1 — Market sizing: estimate total addressable unit sales for this category of game
Step 2 — Market share: estimate the new company's realistic share in year 1
Step 3 — Revenue: price per unit × unit sales
Step 4 — Variable costs: manufacturing/packaging/shipping + retail margin + consumer marketing charge
Step 5 — Fixed costs / salaries: subtract employee compensation
Step 6 — Net profit and investor return: apply 50% equity stake and compare to $500K investment and alternative 50% ROI ($250K)

questions.prompt: Estimate the total market size (unit sales per year) for this type of computer game.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a market-sizing chain from first principles: US population → age/gender filter → gamer subset → game-type preference → purchases per year. Specific numbers matter less than logical structure. A reasonable answer: 300M total US population → ~100M in 15-35 age group (1/3) → ~50M males → ~10M gamers (20%) → ~2M who would like this specific game type (20%) × 1 game/year = 2 million unit sales per year.

math.setup: US population × fraction aged 15-35 × fraction male × fraction who are gamers × fraction who like this genre × games purchased per year
steps: 10M × 20% = 2M potential buyers of this game type
math.answer: ~2 million unit sales per year for this game category

questions.prompt: Estimate the new company's market share and expected unit sales in year 1.
questions.guidance: With 6 existing titles and this new title there are 7 total. Equal share would be 1/7 ≈ 14%. Since it is year 1, a more conservative 10% is appropriate. 10% × 2M = 200,000 units.

math.setup: (1 / (6 existing titles + 1 new title)) = equal share; apply discount for year-1 ramp
steps: Year-1 conservative estimate = 10% of 2M unit market

questions.guidance: Revenue = 200K × $40 = $8M. Variable costs per unit: manufacturing/packaging/shipping ~$6 (10-15% of $40), retail margin $12 (30% × $40), consumer marketing charge $4 (10% × $40). Contribution margin = $40 - $6 - $12 - $4 = $18. Total contribution = 200K × $18 = $3.6M. Fixed costs = $0. Salaries = 2 × $100K = $200K. Net profit = $3.6M - $200K = $3.4M.

math.setup: Revenue - variable costs - salaries = net profit

questions.prompt: Should you invest in the gaming company or the alternative investment?
questions.guidance: Investor's 50% share of $3.4M profit = $1.7M return on a $500K investment, which is a 340% ROI. The alternative yields 50% ROI = $250K return. The gaming company projected return ($1.7M) is more than three times the initial investment and far exceeds the alternative ($250K). Recommendation: invest in the gaming company, subject to acknowledging the key risks (market sizing assumptions, first-year market-share achievement, variable cost estimates).

math.setup: Investor return = net profit × 50% equity stake; compare to alternative: $500K × 50% ROI
math.answer: Gaming investment projected return ($1.7M) exceeds the alternative ($250K) by ~$1.45M; invest in the gaming company

recommendation: Invest in the gaming company: projected first-year return of $1.7M on a $500K investment (340% ROI) versus $250K from the alternative (50% ROI)
The gaming company outperforms the alternative by approximately $1.45M under base-case assumptions
risks: Market-sizing assumptions may be optimistic — actual gamer penetration or genre preference could be lower
10% year-1 market share is aggressive for a new entrant with no brand recognition
Variable cost estimate ($6/unit for manufacturing/packaging/shipping) is rough and could be higher
Revenue is entirely dependent on a single title; no diversification
The founder's ability to execute on marketing and distribution is unproven
next_steps: Validate unit cost estimates with contract manufacturers before committing capital
Confirm retail distribution agreements and actual margin/fee terms with key retailers
Conduct consumer research to stress-test genre demand and willingness to pay $40
Establish milestone-based funding tranches rather than committing the full $500K upfront
